title: Najdorf: critical sidelines and move-order tricks
question: After 5...a6, what do the sixth moves other than the main two ask of Black, what is the best answer to each, and which move orders lead to the same position?
outcomes: Says what 6.Be2, 6.h3, 6.Bc4 and 6.Be3 each prepare and names a good reply to each, with the engine evidence
Explains why ...b5 gains time against a bishop on c4 and not against one on b3
Avoids the tempting but weak moves 7.Nf5 and 7.Bxe6 and the trap 7...e6 after 6.Be3 Ng4 7.Bg5
Recognises one position reached by three move orders (Najdorf, Scheveningen, Kan) and by two (Najdorf, Sozin)
Reads master counts as results with a sample size and not as verdicts

steps.text: **The question of this lesson.** After 5...a6 White has more than a dozen reasonable sixth moves, and each asks Black something different. By the end you can say, for six of them, what the move is for, which reply is best and which plausible reply fails, and you can tell when two move orders arrive at the same position. [V] means checked here, [I] inference, [H] hypothesis.

steps.caption: What strong players chose (our file: 329,379 games, both players 2500+, 2012 to 2026). After 5...a6: 6.Be3 in 2,669 games, 6.Bg5 1,589, 6.Be2 1,371, 6.h3 1,286, 6.g3 537, 6.f3 528, 6.Bd3 522, 6.a4 357, 6.Bc4 334. A count is a menu, not a ranking.

steps.text: **Three questions to ask of any sixth move [I].** First: does it allow or stop ...e5? Second: where does the other bishop go, and does that cost time? Third: after a knight leaves c3, who still guards the e4 pawn? The boards ahead put these questions to Be2, h3, Bc4 and Be3, one move at a time.

**6.Be2: wait, then castle.** The bishop steps in so White can castle at once, and the c1 bishop can still choose e3 or g5 later. It does not stop ...e5, so White is ready to meet that pawn with Nb3. [I] A player who wants a calm structure first chooses it.

steps.text: **Plans in this structure [I].** White: keep the knight on b3, bring the c1 bishop to e3, then the queen to d3 or d2, and aim at the d5 square, which no black pawn can guard now that the c-pawn is gone. Black: develop the c8 bishop to e6, put a knight on d7 or c6, and use the open c-file with a rook. Neither plan is forced; they are what the pawns point to.

steps.text: **6.h3: take g4 away.** [I] The pawn takes g4 away from ...Ng4 and ...Bg4 for as long as it stays on h3, and prepares g4 itself, a pawn advance that needs no f3 and no queen move. In our master file 6.h3 was played 1,286 times; Black answered ...e5 707 times and ...e6 437 times.

steps.text: **What h3 teaches [H].** If a quiet-looking pawn move prepares a pawn advance, the quiet move is half of a plan. Check what the pawn stands behind before you call the move slow.

**6.Bc4: aim at e6.** [I] The bishop looks at e6 and f7, as in the older Sozin Sicilian [R]. The price: ...b5 hits it with a gain of time, so White must know where it retreats. In 334 master games Black answered ...e6 in 321.

steps.text: **What the sacrifice shows [I].** A sacrifice on e6 needs more attackers than defenders and a second wave of pieces. With the king still in the middle and Black's pieces untouched, the second wave is missing. Count first, then sacrifice.

**6.Be3: the English Attack family.** The most played sixth move. The bishop leaves c1 for e3, where it guards d4 and prepares f3, Qd2 and a kingside pawn advance. The answer depends on Black's pawn move. Master file: ...e5 1,546, ...Ng4 673, ...e6 370.

steps.text: **Best answers: a summary [I].** Against Be2, ...e5 and a calm structure. Against h3, ...e6 or ...e5. Against Bc4, ...e6 and the pawn on e6 as a shield, with ...b5 at the right moment. Against Be3, the answer depends on which black pawn moves: ...e5 forces the knight to retreat, ...Ng4 attacks the bishop, ...e6 invites f3 and the pawn storm. Each Black reply is a structure choice.

**One position, many roads.** The position decides the game, not the path. We replayed the move orders below with python-chess [V] and compared the full position after the last move. Three roads from other Sicilians arrive at Najdorf positions of this lesson.

steps.caption: Three move orders, one position. Najdorf: 1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5.Nc3 a6 6.Be2 e6. steps.text: **Why transpositions matter [I].** A player who has learned a move list is lost when the order changes; a player who has learned the position meets it by any road. Before you answer a move, ask what the position is, not which line you studied. It also means one choice can steer Black into a different Sicilian family: with ...Nc6 early or ...e6 first the Najdorf is a choice, not a given.

steps.chapter: Test yourself and teach it back

steps.text: **Recap: what to remember.** Each sixth move asks Black a question about the e5 square, the b5 pawn or the g4 square. Be2 and Nb3 are quiet; h3 takes g4 away and prepares g4; Bc4 aims at e6 and needs Bb3 when ...b5 comes. After Be3 the black pawn move decides the set-up. Do not jump to f5. Do not move the e7 pawn when the f6 square is empty and a bishop on g5 looks at your queen. And the position, not the move order, is what matters.
